section_summary: This final section chiefly concerns Florida protests against scrap-iron shipments to Japan and the Roosevelt administration’s ensuing export-licensing and embargo policy. It also contains a warning relayed through Madrid that restrictions on essential supplies, especially gasoline, could lead to war. The last page shifts to a June 1941 assessment of Japan’s likely response to the German attack on the Soviet Union, including whether Japan might attack Siberia.

subfiles.title: Letter from Senator Charles O. Andrews forwarding protests against scrap-iron shipments
subfiles.about: Senator Andrews forwards two telegrams from Florida organizations protesting the loading of scrap iron for export.
subfiles.summary: Andrews tells Hull that two organizations in his state have protested a shipment of scrap iron then being loaded at a Florida port. He forwards their telegrams for the Secretary’s attention. The page bears October 1940 receipt and filing annotations.

subfiles.title: Duplicate of Senator Andrews’s letter forwarding scrap-iron protests
subfiles.about: A duplicate copy records Andrews’s transmittal of two Florida protests against a scrap-iron shipment.
subfiles.summary: This page duplicates the October 4 letter appearing on page 297. Andrews forwards two protest telegrams concerning scrap iron being loaded at a Florida port and asks that they receive the State Department’s attention.

subfiles.title: Telegram from the Carl Vogel Unit protesting scrap-iron exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Helen McCoy, Secretary, Carl Vogel Unit Number 47, American Legion Auxiliary
subfiles.about: The American Legion Auxiliary unit at Lake Worth asks Andrews to oppose present and future scrap-iron shipments from Palm Beach to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Helen McCoy reports that the members of Carl Vogel Unit Number 47 adopted a resolution protesting current and future shipments of scrap iron to Japan from the port of Palm Beach. The unit requests Senator Andrews’s cooperation.

subfiles.title: Telegram from the Florida Federation of Labor protesting scrap-iron shipments
subfiles.from: Charles E. Silva, President, Florida Federation of Labor
subfiles.about: Silva asks Andrews to prevent scrap-iron cargoes from leaving several Florida ports for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Silva reports protests from organizations in West Palm Beach against scrap iron being loaded on a Greek steamer bound for Japan. The vessel was expected to load additional scrap at Fort Lauderdale and Jacksonville, while a Japanese vessel was also loading scrap at Tampa. The Florida Federation of Labor joins the protest and requests action to stop the shipments.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply on United States scrap-iron export policy
subfiles.to: Charles O. Andrews, United States Senate
subfiles.about: Hull explains the President’s restrictions on exports of iron and steel scrap and returns the two Florida protest telegrams.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that the President’s press announcement sets out the government’s policy on iron and steel scrap exports. Existing licenses were cancelled on October 1, and from October 16 all scrap would require licenses issued only for destinations in the Western Hemisphere and Great Britain. Hull encloses the White House release and implementing instructions to customs collectors, and returns Andrews’s two telegrams.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Madrid reporting a Japanese warning about embargo measures
subfiles.about: An unnamed Japanese naval attaché warns that continued American restrictions on essential exports to Japan would result in war.
subfiles.summary: The reporting officer says the American naval attaché received a lengthy, unannounced visit from the Japanese naval attaché in Madrid. Acting under instructions from his ministry, the Japanese officer declared that “Japan must live” and warned that continued restrictions on essential materials—especially gasoline—would lead to war. The telegram was marked for close paraphrase before disclosure.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Madrid telegram concerning Japanese reaction to embargoes
subfiles.about: This paraphrase restates the Japanese naval attaché’s warning that American export restrictions could produce war.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase records an unannounced visit by the Japanese naval attaché in Madrid to his American counterpart. The Japanese officer, speaking on ministerial instructions, said Japan had to live and that continued United States embargo measures on essential materials, particularly gasoline, would result in war.

subfiles.title: Transmittal memorandum on probable Japanese reactions to the German-Soviet war
subfiles.to: Unstated; copies to Mr. Hornbeck and Mr. Atherton
subfiles.about: The memorandum forwards two preliminary assessments of Japan’s likely response to war between Germany and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The first attached assessment, prepared by Mr. Schmidt and endorsed by senior Division of Far Eastern Affairs officers, is described as the most probable analysis of Japanese reactions. A second assessment by Mr. Langdon outlines factors that might deter Japan from attacking Siberia. Although the writer regards Langdon’s factors as one-sided, both papers indicate that Japan would probably enter a period of uncertainty and great difficulty in choosing its future course.
